newsitem.title: USA: Mideast peace spotlight switches to Washington.
newsitem.headline: Mideast peace spotlight switches to Washington.

text.p: The Middle East spotlight switches to the United States this weekend with an all-out effort by Washington to bring feuding Israelis and Palestinians back to the negotiating table.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu flies in from Israel on Sunday and is expected to come under heavy pressure from U.S. President Bill Clinton at a White House meeting on Monday to make a gesture that would allow talks to resume.
The peace process has ground to a halt since a January agreement whereby Israeli troops withdrew from most of the West Bank town of Hebron.

Palestinian anger over an Israeli decision last month to break ground on a housing project in mainly Arab East Jerusalem has blocked the start of talks meant to decide the "final status" of Palestinian self-rule areas.

Describing this as "one of the most serious moments in the history of the peace process", U.S. officials said they had ideas for breaking the deadlock that would be put to Netanyahu and, by telephone, to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
"We're very active," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said. "We are developing our own ideas and we're going to put them forward." He declined to give details.
The Palestinians say that before Arafat will meet Netanyahu, Israel must stop work on its new housing project -- something the Israeli leader has vowed not to do.

Israel, for its part, says it will not resume negotiations until Arafat orders an end to the West Bank riots that have continued for more than two weeks in protest at the housing start at Jabal Abu Ghneim, called Har Homa by Israel.
But Netanyahu has also put forward a proposal for rapid final status negotiations to wind up in six months, instead of the original 1999 deadline.
If the talks bog down he has suggested a Camp David style summit -- along the lines of the one that produced Israel's peace agreement with Egypt in 1978 -- between himself, Arafat and Clinton.
U.S. officials have so far said this suggestion is premature, and Palestinians have greeted it with outright scepticism given the complexity of such issues as boundaries, refugees and Jerusalem.

Jordan, however, believes Arafat would be wise to take up Netanyahu on his offer of rapid talks -- provided the Palestinians can get a clear idea from Israel of the terms of reference of the negotiations.

Netanyahu will start his visit with a trip to Minnesota to see King Hussein of Jordan, who is undergoing surgery there, flying on to Washington late on Sunday night. Apart from Clinton he will meet Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and address Jewish groups.

In advance of the talks, U.S. officials have urged Arafat to clamp down on violence and terror. But they have also skirmished with Israel over the contentious issue of Jewish settlements, both at Har Homa and on the West Bank.

Albright said on Friday she had expressed concerns to visiting Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai over the "thickening" of West Bank settlements by the building of new housing units within them.

"It is a very delicate moment in the whole situation where it's very important to do everything we can to rebuild the bonds of confidence and to get back to where we are dealing with a way to ultimately get a comprehensive peace," she told reporters.
